issues.legal_issue: A Labour Court may not reduce dismissal for serious proved misconduct by exercising its discretion without reasoned, case-specific grounds, particularly where the misconduct has caused the employer a genuine loss of confidence.
material_facts: The employee had obtained a loan by depositing title deeds as security, but the deeds were taken from the employer’s custody without its knowledge or consent while the mortgage remained in force.
The employee used the deeds to invite offers for the sale of the mortgaged property and sought to justify their possession with a letter bearing forged signatures.
The findings that the misconduct was proved and that the employer’s confidence in the employee had been shaken were not displaced.

The Labour Court reduced dismissal to reinstatement as a fresh candidate, relying on the absence of earlier misconduct and the employee’s participation in cultural and employee activities, despite its findings about the misconduct and loss of confidence.

No court found on the record that the dismissal was vindictive or that the punishment was shockingly disproportionate. The High Court upheld the Labour Court’s order on the erroneous basis that its discretion was unlimited.
issues.conclusion: The Labour Court’s order directing reinstatement was set aside, and the employer’s dismissal order was upheld.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11-A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 does not confer unlimited or arbitrary discretion. The Labour Court must exercise its power judicially, on justifiable grounds supported by material and reasons, and explain any departure from a proper finding of misconduct. Where serious misconduct causes a genuine loss of confidence, reinstatement is not justified merely by a clean prior record or other general mitigating circumstances; interference requires a supported finding that the punishment is vindictive or shockingly disproportionate. The Court applied Air India Corporation v. V.A. Rebellow, Francis Klein & Company Private Limited v. Their Workmen, Janata Bazaar South Kanara Central Co-operative Wholesale Stores Limited v. Secretary, Sahakari Noukarara Sangha, UPSRTC v. Mohan Lal Gupta, Workmen of Firestone Tyre & Rubber Co. v. Management, and CMC Hospital Employees’ Union v. CMC Vellore Association.

rule.if: labour_court_reviewed_dismissal_for_proven_misconduct and unauthorized_removal_of_entrusted_documents and documents_used_to_attempt_property_sale and fabricated_evidence_used_to_justify_removal and employer_genuinely_lost_confidence and labour_court_reduced_dismissal and mitigation_limited_to_clean_prior_record_and_employee_activities and not punishment_found_vindictive_or_shockingly_disproportionate

predicates.labour_court_reviewed_dismissal_for_prov: A Labour Court reviewed an employer’s dismissal of an employee after finding the charged misconduct proved.
predicates.unauthorized_removal_of_entrusted_docume: The employee removed documents entrusted to the employer’s custody without the employer’s knowledge or consent.
predicates.documents_used_to_attempt_property_sale: The employee used the removed documents to attempt a sale of property that remained subject to security for a loan.
predicates.fabricated_evidence_used_to_justify_remo: The employee relied on evidence with forged signatures to claim the documents had been returned with the employer’s permission.
predicates.employer_genuinely_lost_confidence: The employer genuinely lost confidence in the employee because of the proved misconduct.
predicates.labour_court_reduced_dismissal: The Labour Court reduced the employer’s dismissal penalty and ordered reinstatement.
predicates.mitigation_limited_to_clean_prior_record: The Labour Court relied on the absence of earlier misconduct and the employee’s participation in cultural or employee activities as reasons to reduce the penalty.
predicates.punishment_found_vindictive_or_shockingl: A court found on the record that the punishment was vindictive or shockingly disproportionate.

issues.definition: When a Labour Court reduces dismissal in a review of proved misconduct involving unauthorized removal and misuse of entrusted documents, fabricated justification, and genuine loss of employer confidence, general mitigating circumstances alone do not justify that reduction if no court finds the punishment vindictive or shockingly disproportionate; the dismissal is upheld.
